clue.text: Crop brassica from frames

indicators.note: the phrase frames, or encloses, the answer

explanation.surface: A gardener lifting cabbages out of cold frames.
explanation.walkthrough: In the vegetable-plot picture 'Crop' is a harvest; here it is a haircut, and 'frames' is doing the enclosing.
explanation.definitionFit: A crop is a short haircut, and an Afro is a hairstyle.

clue.text: 'Womaniser with band!' It's what they called Mozart

parts.note: a wolf is a man who chases women
a gang is a band of people

explanation.surface: A gossipy remark that the composer Mozart had a reputation as a ladies' man with a band.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface plays on Mozart's famously racy reputation; the definition is a whole phrase pointing to his first name.
explanation.definitionFit: Mozart's first name was Wolfgang.

clue.text: Pine tar soap finally running out

indicators.note: the letter runs out of the word, leaving it

parts.note: pitch is a black tarry substance, used like tar

indicators.note: finally picks out the last letter of the word before it

explanation.surface: Pine tar soap, a real product, is nearly used up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pine' looks like part of the product name, but it is the definition. 'finally' takes the last letter of soap, P, and 'running out' drops it from PITCH.
explanation.definitionFit: To itch for something is to long or yearn for it, as to pine for it.

clue.text: Bound to be penny amongst swept up leaves

indicators.note: in a down answer, 'up' turns the word round

parts.note: leaves = departs, as a train leaves; read upwards in a down entry
p = penny, the abbreviation on British coins, slipped in among the reversed letters

explanation.surface: Someone sweeping up autumn leaves and finding a penny among them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Leaves' looks like foliage but is the verb departs; 'swept up' makes it read backwards in this down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: Tied down with straps, the literal sense of bound; the surface's 'bound to be' hides it as a phrase meaning certain.

clue.text: Fighting in Metro regularly upset underground network

indicators.note: in a down clue, upset means turned upside down, so the letters run the other way
regularly takes every other letter of the words that follow

explanation.surface: Violence breaks out on the Metro, disrupting the underground rail network.
explanation.walkthrough: 'regularly' takes the second, fourth and sixth letters of 'in Metro', NER, and 'upset' turns them round to REN. 'underground network' suggests a metro system, but it is a network of burrows.
explanation.definitionFit: A warren is a network of interconnecting rabbit burrows dug beneath the ground.

clue.text: Foreign expat nobly yielding section of field

indicators.note: foreign means strange, so the letters come out altered

explanation.surface: An expatriate abroad graciously giving up a patch of farmland.
explanation.walkthrough: The field sounds agricultural; it is a football pitch, where the penalty box is the marked area in front of goal.
explanation.definitionFit: On a football pitch this is the marked rectangle in front of each goal, one section of the field of play.

clue.text: Drunk husband drinking more getting half-cut in plane

parts.note: first half of MORE, placed inside SOT: S(MO)OT

explanation.surface: A drunken husband getting more and more tipsy on a flight.
explanation.walkthrough: The plane is not an aircraft but the carpenter's verb; 'half-cut', British slang for drunk, is really an instruction to halve MORE.
explanation.definitionFit: A carpenter's plane shaves wood flat, so as a verb plane is a plain synonym for making even.

clue.text: Princess forbidden to go out of bounds

indicators.note: the bounds of a word are its outer letters, and both go out

explanation.surface: A princess is forbidden to stray past the palace limits.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out of bounds' reads as a restricted area, but it strips the first and last letters from BANNED. Princess Anne is the Princess Royal, sister of King Charles III.
explanation.definitionFit: Anne, the Princess Royal, is the only daughter of Queen Elizabeth II and a British princess.

clue.text: Cafe's penultimate potato dish; one's left in reserve

indicators.note: penultimate means second to last, the letter before the final one

parts.note: the word café, its 's read as is

indicators.note: left as in departed, so the letter leaves the dish

parts.note: rösti is a Swiss dish of fried grated potato
one is I, the Roman numeral, and the 's reads as is

explanation.surface: A café's last-but-one potato dish is set aside in reserve.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cafe's' reads 'Cafe is': its 'penultimate' letter is F. 'one's left' means I has gone from ROSTI, leaving ROST. 'reserve' looks like a store, but it is a manner.
explanation.definitionFit: Frost can mean coldness of manner, an icy reserve or aloofness shown towards someone.

clue.text: Cabinetmakers, perhaps, or carpenters smartened up?

indicators.note: smartened is stirred up into a new order

explanation.surface: Woodworkers who have tidied themselves up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Smartened up' reads as one phrasal verb; split it, and 'up' stirs the letters of SMARTENED.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by example: cabinetmakers and carpenters are both skilled manual workers who follow a trade.

clue.text: Article penned by sour character not being broadcast

parts.note: an air is a manner or character

explanation.surface: A newspaper article written by a sour personality that never gets published.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Penned' suggests writing the article; it means enclosed. 'Sour character' looks like one grumpy person but is two pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom from radio and television: a programme off the air is not currently being transmitted.

clue.text: All-rounder oddly only making single

indicators.note: take the odd-numbered letters

explanation.surface: A cricket all-rounder who managed only a single run.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket an all-rounder bats and bowls, and a single is one run; here 'single' means unaccompanied.
explanation.definitionFit: Single, as in on one's own, means alone.

clue.text: Son snubbed fish, going back for other seafood

indicators.note: snubbed puns on snub, short
the shortened fish is read backwards

parts.note: pollack is a sea fish; drop the K, then reverse POLLAC to CALLOP

explanation.surface: A son rejecting the fish on his plate and ordering some other seafood instead.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Snubbed' reads as rejected; here it means docked, as in a snub nose.
explanation.definitionFit: A scallop is a shellfish, a seafood other than the fish already used.

clue.text: Goals for goalies but not for strikers?

definitions.meaning: read as the football scores a goalkeeper concedes, and meant as the aims a goalkeeper has
a striker wants the ball in the net, so every stop by the keeper thwarts them

explanation.surface: A football pundit's quip about what each player wants.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Goals' here means aims: a goalkeeper aims to make saves, which a striker never wants to see.
explanation.definitionFit: A goalkeeper's stops are what they aim for, and each one denies a striker, so both halves of the clue point at the same act.

clue.text: Cheese from a can spread with relish

indicators.note: the letters are spread about into a new order

parts.note: anagram fodder, joined 'with' the first part

explanation.surface: Tinned cheese spread smeared on with pickle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spread' and 'relish' feel like sandwich fillings; one stirs the letters and the other is fodder. Lancashire is an English county that names a crumbly cheese.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by example: this crumbly white cheese takes its name from the county in north-west England where it is made.

clue.text: Nicked, distinguished companion is put inside

indicators.note: British slang for jailed, used literally

parts.note: CH = Companion of Honour, a British order

explanation.surface: A notable's companion arrested and jailed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nicked' and 'put inside' are British slang for arrested and jailed; here nicked means cut with a small notch.
explanation.definitionFit: Nicked in the sense of cut with a small V-shaped mark; the surface pushes the slang sense of arrested.

clue.text: Act after act succeeded … they're all dead now

parts.note: a second DO follows the first
s = succeeded, as in family trees

explanation.surface: A long variety show running act after act until the audience has expired.
explanation.walkthrough: The dodo is the proverbial extinct bird, hence 'all dead now'.
explanation.definitionFit: The flightless bird of Mauritius is the byword for extinction, as in 'dead as a dodo', so 'all dead now' fits.

clue.text: A choosy eater, teenage visitor returned sandwiches

indicators.note: the hidden letters read backwards
the words sandwich the answer between them

parts.note: the letters run across the end of teenage and the start of visitor, then read backwards

explanation.surface: A fussy teenage guest sending back the sandwiches.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sandwiches' looks like the food sent back; it is the verb, holding the answer inside.
explanation.definitionFit: A vegan chooses carefully what to eat, avoiding all animal products.

clue.text: Shorten short dwarf

parts.note: to dock is to shorten; remove the final K

explanation.surface: Cutting a small person down to size.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Short' looks like part of the definition beside 'dwarf'; it is the instruction to cut DOCK.
explanation.definitionFit: Doc is one of the Seven Dwarfs in Snow White.

clue.text: Top performers at most AGMs — the Chippendales?

definitions.meaning: the people chairing a company's annual general meeting, its most senior figures
read as the male strip troupe, but meant as the followers of Thomas Chippendale, the 18th-century furniture maker who made chairs

explanation.surface: A cheeky suggestion that the Chippendales strip troupe are the star turns at company meetings.
explanation.walkthrough: The Chippendales are male strippers, but Chippendale was also an 18th-century furniture maker, so they are chair men. An AGM is a company's annual general meeting.
explanation.definitionFit: Those who chair meetings are chairmen, and Chippendale's craftsmen made chairs, so the second sense is a punning one flagged by the question mark.

clue.text: Man perhaps in offer to host Games

explanation.surface: A city bidding to host the Games.
explanation.walkthrough: The bid to host the Games reads like an Olympic bid; Games is school PE.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by example, flagged by 'perhaps': humans walk on two feet, so man is one kind of two-legged animal.

clue.text: State benefits: who can say what the future holds?

definitions.text: who can say what the future holds?

indicators.note: to state is to say out loud

explanation.surface: A political question about welfare payments and whether anyone can predict them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'State benefits' reads as welfare; 'State' is split off as the say-it instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: Seers who foretell events are the people who can say what lies ahead, and the question mark marks the definition as a description.

clue.text: Waterproofing marine network will take time

definitions.note: Waterproofing is used as a noun, the material.

explanation.surface: Weatherproofing an undersea cable network will be a slow job.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Marine network' looks like one thing; it breaks into SEA and LAN.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym for the noun: the paste or coating used for waterproofing a joint is what this names.

clue.text: Sinatra cryptically leading line of stars!

parts.note: read cryptically, Sinatra splits as S IN ATRA, an instruction to put S inside ATRA; that result leads, coming before L for line

explanation.surface: Frank Sinatra, as a star, heads a line of celebrities.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cryptically' asks you to read the singer's name as a set of instructions: S in ATRA gives ASTRA, then L, the usual abbreviation for line, follows.
explanation.definitionFit: Astral is the adjective of the stars, from the Latin astrum, as in astral bodies.

clue.text: Kicking GTI, one's in a rage

indicators.note: the letters are thrown about wildly

explanation.surface: An angry motorist kicking his GTI hatchback.
explanation.walkthrough: A GTI is a sporty car model; here its letters are simply fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Toeing a ball is striking it with the tip of the boot, a particular way of kicking.

clue.text: Worried by debts one's taken on in advance

parts.note: x = by, as in 3 x 4 metres
IOUs are written promises to pay debts

explanation.surface: Someone fretting over debts taken on before being paid.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Worried by debts' reads as one idea; 'by' is its own piece, the multiplication sign in dimensions.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: someone fretting over debts is uneasy, nervous, worried.

clue.text: Lucifer's rival

definitions.meaning: read as the Devil, but meant as the Victorian name for a strike-anywhere light for fires and pipes
an equal or opponent, someone able to compete on level terms

explanation.surface: Who could be a match for the Devil?
explanation.walkthrough: Lucifer is the Devil, but a lucifer was also an old name for a friction match.
explanation.definitionFit: A lucifer was a Victorian friction match, and a match is also an equal who can compete with you; the two senses share the word.

clue.text: Married woman captures the heart of karaoke bar

definitions.note: The definition names the thing; the answer is its brand name.

indicators.note: captures as in takes prisoner

parts.note: Mrs is a married woman's title

indicators.note: the heart is the centre, so take karaoke's middle letter

explanation.surface: A wife stealing the show at a karaoke bar.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Karaoke bar' reads as a venue; 'bar' is split off, and a Mars bar is a British chocolate bar.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by brand: a Mars is the best-known British chocolate bar, so 'bar' names it by its shape.

clue.text: Carpets are being ruined by parties

indicators.note: by means next to, so the parties follow the jumbled word
something being ruined is wrecked and broken up, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Rugs are spoiled by guests at parties.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Carpets' looks like the rugs, but it is the verb: to carpet someone is British slang for to reprimand them. 'being ruined' shuffles ARE to EAR, and 'by' places BASHES after it.
explanation.definitionFit: To earbash someone is informal for lecturing or scolding them at length, as carpeting a person does.

clue.text: Angel wanting massage? It's beyond a desire

definitions.note: Desire is read as a verb, to long for.

indicators.note: wanting in its sense of lacking: the angel is missing the massage
beyond means further along, so the remains come after A

parts.note: a cherub is an angel; remove RUB
a rub is a massage, taken away from CHERUB to leave CHE

explanation.surface: An angel longing for a massage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wanting massage' reads as longing for one; 'wanting' means lacking, and 'It' is the leftover CHE.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym for the verb: to long for something is to have a nagging want of it, the sense of 'desire'.

clue.text: Special key needed for compound

parts.note: the Alt key on a keyboard

explanation.surface: A particular key needed to get into a walled compound.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Compound' suggests an enclosure; it is the chemical sense, and salts are compounds.
explanation.definitionFit: A salt is a chemical compound, such as sodium chloride.

clue.text: Back boiler put in new position

parts.note: a range is a kitchen stove that can also heat water

explanation.surface: A plumber moving the back boiler somewhere else.
explanation.walkthrough: A back boiler sits behind a fire to heat water; split it and 'boiler' is a range cooker.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym for the verb: moving furniture into a new position is to reorder it.

clue.text: Fashionable English learner driver's one after Golf?

parts.note: the L-plate on a learner driver's car

explanation.surface: A trendy English learner driver hoping to take up golf.
explanation.walkthrough: In the NATO alphabet Hotel follows Golf; the question mark flags that this is one example.
explanation.definitionFit: In the phonetic alphabet, Hotel is the word after Golf.
